subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Biology Reproduction Reading
subtitle: Reading practice on human reproduction, puberty, fertilisation, pregnancy and scientific evidence.
description: Five KS3 reading passages for biology reproduction. The passages support factual recall, inference, explanation and data interpretation using respectful scientific language.

data.sourcePassage: Reproduction is the biological process by which living things produce new individuals. Humans reproduce sexually, which means two specialised sex cells, called gametes, are involved. The male gamete is a sperm cell and the female gamete is an egg cell. Each gamete contains genetic information. During fertilisation, the nucleus of one sperm cell joins with the nucleus of one egg cell. This forms a fertilised egg cell called a zygote. Sexual reproduction is different from asexual reproduction because offspring inherit genetic information from two biological parents, not just one parent. This helps explain why children may resemble their biological parents but are not exactly identical to either of them.

questions.question: What is reproduction?
questions.modelAnswer: Reproduction is the biological process by which living things produce new individuals.

questions.question: Which pair are the human gametes?
questions.modelAnswer: Sperm cell and egg cell

questions.question: Why are offspring from sexual reproduction not usually identical to either biological parent?
questions.modelAnswer: They inherit genetic information from two gametes, one from each biological parent.

questions.question: What cell is formed immediately after fertilisation?
questions.modelAnswer: A zygote is formed.

questions.question: Explain the key difference between sexual and asexual reproduction.
questions.modelAnswer: Sexual reproduction involves two gametes joining, while asexual reproduction involves one parent producing offspring without gametes joining.

data.sourcePassage: The male reproductive system produces sperm and transfers semen during sexual reproduction. Sperm are made in the testes, which also produce testosterone. Sperm then move through the sperm ducts. Glands add fluid to sperm to make semen, and semen leaves the body through the urethra and penis. The female reproductive system contains egg cells and can support pregnancy. The ovaries contain egg cells and produce hormones including oestrogen and progesterone. In many menstrual cycles, one ovary releases an egg during ovulation. The egg moves into an oviduct, where fertilisation usually happens if sperm reaches it. The uterus is the organ where an embryo can implant and a fetus can develop. The cervix is the narrow opening below the uterus, and the vagina is a muscular canal that can receive sperm and act as the birth canal.

questions.question: Which organs produce sperm?
questions.modelAnswer: The testes produce sperm.

questions.question: Where does fertilisation usually happen in humans?
questions.modelAnswer: Fertilisation usually happens in an oviduct.

questions.question: Explain why sperm and semen are not the same thing.
questions.modelAnswer: Sperm are cells, while semen is fluid containing sperm and substances added by glands.

questions.question: Name two functions of the ovaries.
questions.modelAnswer: The ovaries contain egg cells, release eggs during ovulation in many cycles, and produce oestrogen and progesterone.

questions.question: A student says fertilisation happens in the uterus. Correct this misconception.
questions.modelAnswer: Fertilisation usually happens in an oviduct. The uterus is where an embryo can implant and a fetus can develop.

data.sourceTitle: Puberty, Hormones and the Menstrual Cycle
data.targetTitle: Puberty, Hormones and the Menstrual Cycle
data.sourcePassage: Puberty is the stage when reproductive organs mature and the body becomes capable of reproduction. It starts at different ages and progresses at different speeds for different people. Adolescence includes puberty but is wider: it also includes emotional and social development between childhood and adulthood. Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood. Testosterone is produced mainly by the testes and is linked to sperm production and many male puberty changes. Oestrogen and progesterone are produced by the ovaries and help control female puberty changes, the menstrual cycle and pregnancy. The menstrual cycle is a repeated cycle of changes in the ovaries and uterus. Menstruation is the loss of the uterus lining through the vagina, while ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. A 28-day cycle is a useful model, but real cycles can be shorter or longer.

questions.question: What is puberty?
questions.modelAnswer: Puberty is the stage when reproductive organs mature and the body becomes capable of reproduction.

questions.question: Which hormone is strongly linked to sperm production?
questions.modelAnswer: Testosterone

questions.question: Explain why adolescence is not exactly the same as puberty.
questions.modelAnswer: Puberty is reproductive maturation, while adolescence also includes emotional and social development between childhood and adulthood.

questions.question: How are menstruation and ovulation different?
questions.modelAnswer: Menstruation is loss of the uterus lining through the vagina, while ovulation is release of an egg from an ovary.

questions.question: Why is it better to describe puberty using age ranges rather than one fixed age?
questions.modelAnswer: Puberty begins and progresses at different ages and speeds for different people, so one fixed age would be misleading.

data.sourcePassage: Fertilisation is the joining of the nucleus of a sperm cell with the nucleus of an egg cell. In humans, it usually happens in an oviduct. The fertilised egg cell, or zygote, divides by cell division to form an embryo. The embryo can implant in the uterus lining. Pregnancy requires both fertilisation and implantation; it does not begin every time sperm enters the body. During pregnancy, the embryo develops in the uterus and is later called a fetus. The fetus does not breathe air inside the uterus. Oxygen and glucose pass from the mother's blood across the placenta and travel to the fetus through the umbilical cord. Carbon dioxide and urea pass from the fetus towards the mother's blood so they can be removed. The mother's blood and fetus's blood do not normally mix directly. Birth happens when uterus muscles contract, the cervix opens wider and the baby is usually born through the vagina.

questions.question: Where does fertilisation usually happen in humans?
questions.modelAnswer: It usually happens in an oviduct.

questions.question: What connects the fetus to the placenta?
questions.modelAnswer: The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta.

questions.question: Explain why the fetus does not need to breathe air inside the uterus.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen passes from the mother's blood across the placenta and reaches the fetus through the umbilical cord.

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to say pregnancy starts every time sperm enters the body?
questions.modelAnswer: Pregnancy requires fertilisation and implantation. Not every sperm reaches an egg, and not every embryo implants.

questions.question: Describe two directions of substance movement across the placenta.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen and glucose move from mother to fetus, while carbon dioxide and urea move from fetus to mother.

data.sourcePassage: Science lessons on reproduction should use accurate and respectful vocabulary, such as uterus, testes, sperm, egg cell, menstruation and fertilisation. Students should not be asked to share personal information about puberty, periods, family circumstances, pregnancy or medical history. When data are used, they should be anonymised, invented for classroom practice, or taken from published summaries. Safe reproduction-linked investigations can use organisms such as yeast or seeds instead of personal human data. For example, a class might test how temperature affects yeast activity by measuring carbon dioxide produced in ten minutes. Temperature would be the independent variable, carbon dioxide volume would be the dependent variable, and controls could include amount of yeast, sugar concentration, solution volume and time measured. Repeating measurements can improve reliability and help identify anomalous results. When reading diagrams or graphs, students should quote evidence, describe trends using values and avoid making claims beyond the data.

questions.modelAnswer: Examples include uterus, testes, sperm, egg cell, menstruation and fertilisation.

questions.question: In the yeast investigation, what is the independent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature

questions.question: Why is a yeast or seed investigation suitable for school reproduction-linked work?
questions.modelAnswer: It studies reproduction-linked processes without asking students to reveal personal human information.

questions.question: Name two control variables in the yeast investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: Control variables could include amount of yeast, sugar concentration, solution volume and time measured.

questions.question: Explain why students should avoid making claims beyond the data.
questions.modelAnswer: Scientific conclusions should be supported by evidence. Claims beyond the data may be inaccurate because the diagram, graph or dataset may be simplified or limited.
